title: Distributed Key-Value Store
prompt: Design a key-value store that holds a few terabytes across many machines, keeps working when machines or a whole zone fail, and lets each application choose between faster responses and fresher reads.

clarify.q: How many keys, and how big are values on average and at most?
clarify.why: Sets node count and whether values live inline in the storage engine. Values of tens of MB belong in an object store with only a pointer here.

clarify.q: During a network partition, must writes keep working on both sides, or is it fine to reject them?
clarify.why: This is the CAP choice. 'Always writable' leads to leaderless replication with conflict handling. 'Reject rather than diverge' leads to a leader per partition with consensus.

clarify.q: When two clients write the same key at the same time, may one write silently win?
clarify.why: If yes, last-write-wins is enough. If lost updates are unacceptable (a shopping cart, counters), we need version vectors and merge logic, or CRDT values.

clarify.q: Do callers need to read their own writes immediately, or is a short delay fine?
clarify.why: Read-your-writes needs overlapping read and write quorums, or session stickiness. A short delay allows reading a single replica at much lower latency.

clarify.q: What are the read and write rates, and the latency targets?
clarify.why: Sets R and W defaults, the storage engine (an LSM tree is good for heavy writes) and how much of the hot set must sit in memory.

clarify.q: Do we need range scans, secondary indexes or multi-key transactions?
clarify.why: Hash partitioning makes point lookups even but destroys key order. Range scans need order-preserving partitioning; transactions need a different system.
Cross-region links add 70–150 ms. Synchronous quorums across regions make every write that slow, so regions usually replicate asynchronously.

functional: get(key), put(key, value), delete(key); keys up to 256 B, values up to 1 MB; optional TTL per key.
Each request may choose a consistency level: ONE, QUORUM or ALL.
Concurrent writes are never silently merged unless the table is configured for last-write-wins; otherwise a read returns all conflicting versions with a context to merge them.
Nodes can be added or removed without downtime; data rebalances automatically.
Replicas that missed writes catch up automatically, with no operator action.
nonFunctional: Latency at QUORUM inside one region: get p99 under 10 ms, put p99 under 15 ms.
Reads and writes at QUORUM keep working with any one replica of each key down, including a full availability zone outage.
An acknowledged QUORUM write survives the permanent loss of any one node.
Capacity grows linearly by adding nodes: 4.2 TB of data now, 10× within three years.
Replicas converge within seconds normally, and within one repair cycle (7 days) in the worst case.
outOfScope: Strongly consistent replication across regions (regions replicate asynchronously).

assumptions: 2 B keys; average key 50 B, value 2 KB, about 2.1 KB per record with version metadata
Replication factor N = 3, one replica per availability zone
Nodes with 2 TB NVMe, kept under 50% full for compaction and rebuild headroom
LSM storage engine with about 30% space overhead and about 10× write amplification from compaction

steps.label: On disk with replicas and overhead
steps.math: 4.2 TB × 3 replicas = 12.6 TB; × 1.3 LSM overhead ≈ 16.4 TB

steps.label: Node count
steps.math: 16.4 TB / 1 TB usable per node ≈ 16.4 → round up to a multiple of 3 zones
steps.result: 18 nodes, 6 per zone, about 0.9 TB each

steps.label: Disk write bandwidth per node
steps.result: ≈ 175 MB/s of disk writes per node: fine on NVMe, not on network disks

steps.label: Hints while one node is down for an hour
steps.result: ≈ 63 GB of hints spread over the other nodes

steps.label: Availability of a 2-of-3 quorum
steps.math: Node down with p = 0.001: P(≥ 2 down) = 3p²(1 − p) + p³ ≈ 3.0 × 10⁻⁶. For W = 3: 0.999³ ≈ 0.997
steps.result: QUORUM ≈ 99.9997% vs ALL ≈ 99.7%, assuming independent failures

estimates.takeaway:
The data is not huge: 18 nodes hold it with room to grow. The interesting numbers are about failure. A 2-of-3 quorum is about 1 000× less likely to be unavailable than requiring all 3 replicas (3 × 10⁻⁶ vs 3 × 10⁻³). That is the whole argument for quorums.

One node down for an hour creates 63 GB of hints, so hinted handoff needs a time limit, with Merkle-tree repair for longer outages. The 175 MB/s of compaction writes per node is why we insist on local NVMe disks.

api.note: context is an opaque encoding of the version vector. Clients pass it back on their next write so the store knows what they had seen.

api.returns: 204 + new context · 503 if fewer than W replicas answered
api.note: A write without a context, to a table that keeps siblings, becomes a sibling of whatever exists.
Writes a tombstone, not a physical delete, so replicas that missed the delete cannot bring the value back.
Internal. Reads ask one replica for the full value and the others for a digest only, saving bandwidth.
Merkle-tree comparison used by anti-entropy, walking down only branches that differ.
Each node gossips with 1–3 random peers every second, so membership spreads in O(log n) rounds.

entities.name: Record
entities.store: LSM tree on each replica: commit log, memtable, SSTables with Bloom filters
fields: hashed with Murmur3 to a 64-bit token
depends on the table's conflict mode
entities.why: Writes are appends (commit log + memtable), so 8 300 writes/s per node is cheap. Bloom filters let a read skip SSTables that cannot hold the key.

entities.name: Ring
entities.store: Gossiped between nodes, persisted locally on each
fields: used to place replicas in distinct zones
entities.why: Every node and token-aware client can compute a key's replicas locally, with no lookup service.

entities.name: Hint
entities.store: Local hint log on the node that accepted the write for an absent replica
entities.why: Holds writes for a replica that is briefly down, so it catches up in minutes instead of waiting for a full repair.

data.note: Partitioning is by hash(key), so load is even but key order is lost, which is why range scans are out of scope. With 18 nodes × 256 virtual nodes = 4 608 ranges, each range holds about 2 B / 4 608 ≈ 434 000 keys. That is also the unit of streaming when nodes join and the unit of Merkle-tree repair. Each table picks its conflict mode once, either lww or siblings, because mixing the two on one key is unsafe.

hld.summary:
All nodes are equal: there is no leader and no master. A token-aware client library hashes the key and sends the request to one of its replicas, which acts as the coordinator. The coordinator walks the ring clockwise from the key's token and picks the first 3 distinct physical nodes in 3 different zones. That is the key's preference list. It sends the operation to all 3 and replies once W (writes) or R (reads) have answered.

Each node stores data in an LSM tree. Nodes learn about each other through gossip and judge peers with a failure detector. Three repair mechanisms work at different time scales. Hinted handoff covers seconds to hours, read repair fixes stale replicas that get read, and Merkle-tree anti-entropy covers anything left over, weekly per range.

diagram.title: Coordinator, replicas and repair paths
diagram.src:
flowchart LR
  APP[Application] --> CL["Client library (token-aware)"]
  CL --> CO["Coordinator node"]
  CO --> A["Replica A - zone 1"]
  CO --> B["Replica B - zone 2"]
  CO --> C["Replica C - zone 3"]
  CO -. hint when C is down .-> H[(Hint log)]
  H -. replay when C returns .-> C
  A <-. gossip .-> B
  B <-. gossip .-> C
  AE[Anti-entropy repair] --> A
  AE --> C

flows.title: A QUORUM write
steps: Client hashes the key to a token and sends PUT to replica A, which coordinates.
A attaches a version (increments its own entry in the version vector, or stamps an HLC time) and sends the write to A, B and C in parallel.
Each replica appends to its commit log, inserts into the memtable and acks.
Once 2 acks arrive, A replies 204 with the new context. A slow third replica finishes in the background.
If C does not answer within 2 s, A stores a hint for C, still within the 3-hour window.

flows.title: A QUORUM read with read repair
steps: Coordinator asks the fastest replica for the full value and a second replica for a digest.
If the digests match, return the value. That is the common case.
If they differ, fetch full values from all replicas, resolve them (newest under LWW, or siblings under version vectors) and return the result.
Asynchronously write the resolved version to any replica that was behind.

flows.title: A node joins
steps: New node picks 256 tokens and gossips status 'joining'.
For each range it will own, it streams data from the current replicas, about 1/19 of the cluster's data, roughly 0.86 TB.
While joining, it receives new writes for its ranges as an extra replica, so nothing is missed during streaming.
It switches to 'normal' and the old owners drop the ranges they no longer replicate after a cleanup.

deepDives.title: Partitioning and placing replicas
deepDives.problem: We must spread 2 B keys over 18 nodes, so that adding a 19th node moves only a fair share of data, and so that the 3 replicas of a key never share a failure domain.

options.name: hash(key) mod N
options.how: Node = hash(key) mod number of nodes.
pros: Trivial
Perfectly even
cons: Going from 18 to 19 nodes moves 18/19 ≈ 95% of all keys
No notion of zones

options.name: Consistent hashing, one token per node
options.how: Nodes sit at one point each on a 64-bit ring, and a key belongs to the next node clockwise.
pros: Adding a node moves only the keys in its new arc
cons: With 18 random points, arcs vary a lot, so some nodes own about twice the average
A new node takes all its data from one neighbour, which is slow and uneven

options.name: Consistent hashing with virtual nodes
options.how: Each physical node owns 256 random tokens. Replicas are the next 3 distinct physical nodes clockwise, skipping any node in a zone already used.
pros: Load evens out to within a few percent
A joining node pulls small pieces from every node in parallel
Bigger machines can take more tokens
cons: More ranges to track and repair (4 608)
Placement walks get more complex with zone rules

options.name: Fixed number of partitions
options.how: Split the hash space into 4 096 fixed partitions at creation and assign whole partitions to nodes. Rebalancing moves whole partitions.
pros: Very predictable: a partition is the unit of moving, repair and backup
Easy to reason about who owns what
cons: The partition count is chosen once. Too few and they get huge, too many and per-partition overhead grows
Needs some process to decide assignments

deepDives.choice:
Consistent hashing with 256 virtual nodes per machine and zone-aware replica placement. Adding node 19 moves about 1/19 of the 16.4 TB, roughly 0.86 TB, streamed from all 18 nodes. At 50 MB/s throttled per source that is 900 MB/s in total, so about 16 minutes. Zone awareness means losing a whole zone removes exactly one replica of every key, so QUORUM keeps working.

What would change my mind: if operations prefer explicit control, fixed partitions are equally good and simpler to debug. If we needed range scans, I would switch to range partitioning with split and merge.

deepDives.title: Quorum maths: N, R and W
deepDives.problem: With N = 3 replicas, a write waits for W acks and a read for R answers. The rule R + W > N means every read set overlaps the latest write set in at least one replica. Interviewers push on what that buys, what it does not, and how failures bend it.

options.name: R = 1, W = 1
options.how: Answer as soon as any single replica responds.
pros: Lowest latency, highest availability: works with 2 of 3 replicas down
cons: R + W = 2 ≤ 3: reads can miss the latest write for a while
A write acked by one node is lost if that node dies before replicating

options.name: R = 2, W = 2
options.how: Majority for both reads and writes.
pros: R + W = 4 > 3: a read always touches at least one replica holding the latest acked write
Tolerates one replica down for both reads and writes
An acked write is on 2 nodes in 2 zones
cons: Latency is the second-fastest replica, not the fastest
Still not linearizable (see below)

options.name: R = 1, W = 3
options.how: Writes wait for all replicas; reads ask one.
pros: Fast reads that see every acked write
cons: Any single replica down blocks writes: 99.7% vs 99.9997% availability at p = 0.001

options.name: Sloppy quorum
options.how: If a preference-list replica is down, count an ack from the next healthy node on the ring, which keeps a hint.
pros: Writes keep succeeding even when 2 of 3 home replicas are unreachable
cons: W acks may land on nodes outside the read set, so R + W > N no longer guarantees overlap until the hints are delivered

deepDives.choice:
Default N = 3, R = 2, W = 2 with strict quorums, and let each request lower it. Session caches can read at ONE, and fire-and-forget logs can write at ONE.

Be explicit about what quorums do not give you. A write that reached only 1 replica returns an error but is not rolled back, so later reads may or may not see it. Two concurrent writes can land in different orders on different replicas. A reader during propagation can see the new value, and a later reader can see the old one, until read repair runs. So the guarantee is 'reads see every write acknowledged before the read began', not linearizability.

What would change my mind: a table that needs compare-and-set or uniqueness (usernames). Leaderless quorums cannot do that safely. I would put those keys in a consensus-based store with a Raft group per range.

diagram.title: Write W = 2 and read R = 2 overlap on B
diagram.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant Cl as Client
  participant Co as Coordinator
  participant A as Replica A
  participant B as Replica B
  participant C as Replica C
  Cl->>Co: PUT k = v2
  Co->>A: write v2
  Co->>B: write v2
  Co->>C: write v2
  A-->>Co: ack
  B-->>Co: ack
  Co-->>Cl: 204 after 2 acks
  Note over C: C is slow and still holds v1
  Cl->>Co: GET k
  Co->>B: read
  Co->>C: read
  B-->>Co: v2
  C-->>Co: v1
  Co-->>Cl: v2 is newer
  Co->>C: read repair v2

deepDives.title: Conflicts: last-write-wins or version vectors
deepDives.problem: In a leaderless store, two clients can write the same key through different coordinators at nearly the same time. Both succeed. Later the replicas disagree, and the store must decide whether one write replaces the other or whether both survive until someone merges them.

options.name: Last-write-wins by wall clock
options.how: Each write carries the coordinator's timestamp, and the highest timestamp wins everywhere.
pros: Simple, constant metadata (8 bytes)
Replicas always converge to one value
cons: Concurrent writes silently lose one
Clock skew can drop a write that really happened later: a node 50 ms fast wins against honest nodes for 50 ms

options.name: Last-write-wins by hybrid logical clock
options.how: Timestamps combine physical time with a logical counter, and nodes advance their clock past any timestamp they receive.
pros: Same simplicity
Causally later writes (read, then write) always get a higher timestamp, even across skewed nodes
cons: Truly concurrent writes still lose one silently

options.name: Version vectors with siblings
options.how: Each version carries a map of node → counter. If one vector is ≥ the other in every entry, it replaces it. Otherwise the versions are concurrent, and both are kept as siblings and returned to the client to merge.
pros: Never loses a concurrent write
Precisely separates 'happened after' from 'concurrent'
cons: Every client must handle siblings and write merge logic
Vectors grow with the number of coordinators, so they need pruning, which can create false conflicts
Sibling explosion if clients write blindly without a context

options.name: CRDT values
options.how: Store data types whose merge is built in, such as counters, sets with add and remove, and maps of registers.
pros: Conflicts resolve automatically and correctly for that type
No client merge code
cons: Only works for data that fits a CRDT shape
Metadata overhead, for example per-element tags in sets

deepDives.choice:
Worked example with version vectors. Client 1 writes v1 through node A: [A:1]. Clients 2 and 3 both read v1. Client 2 writes v2 through B: [A:1, B:1]. Client 3 writes v3 through C: [A:1, C:1]. Neither vector dominates, so a read returns siblings {v2, v3}. The client merges them (for a cart, the union) and writes through A with the merged context: [A:2, B:1, C:1], which dominates both, so the siblings disappear. Under LWW, one of the two cart items would have vanished.

My pick: per table. LWW with hybrid logical clocks is the default, because most tables (profiles, sessions, caches) overwrite whole values and nobody minds which of two simultaneous writes wins. Tables where a lost update costs money, such as carts or counters, use CRDT types where they fit, and siblings with version vectors otherwise.

What would change my mind: if client teams cannot be trusted to write merge code, I would offer only LWW and CRDTs, and route anything else to a consensus store.

deepDives.title: Healing: hinted handoff, read repair and anti-entropy
deepDives.problem: Replicas drift: a node reboots and misses 10 minutes of writes, a hint log is lost with its disk, a write reached only 1 replica. Without active repair, a later failure of the up-to-date replica would lose data. Deletes add a trap: a replica that missed a delete can bring the value back.

options.name: Hinted handoff
options.how: When a replica is down, the coordinator keeps the write in a local hint log and replays it once gossip says the replica is back. Hints older than 3 hours are dropped.
pros: Fast catch-up after short outages
Cheap: only the missed writes move
cons: Hints live on one node, so they are lost if that node dies
Unbounded outages mean unbounded hints (63 GB per node-hour at our rate), hence the time cap

options.name: Read repair
options.how: When a read finds replicas disagreeing, write the resolved value back to the stale ones.
pros: Free consistency for data that is actually read
Fixes hot keys quickly
cons: Never touches keys nobody reads
Adds work to the read path on mismatches

options.name: Merkle-tree anti-entropy
options.how: Per range, each replica builds a hash tree over its keys (1 024 leaves of about 424 keys each). Two replicas compare root hashes, walk down only the branches that differ, and stream just the keys under mismatching leaves.
pros: Finds every difference, including keys nobody reads
Moves little data: one differing leaf means about 10 levels of hash comparison and about 0.9 MB of keys, instead of the range's 910 MB
cons: Building trees means reading the whole range: real disk I/O, so it runs throttled and on a schedule
Writes during the scan make trees slightly stale, so some 'differences' are just in-flight writes

deepDives.choice:
All three, by time scale. Hints cover short outages, read repair covers hot data, and a full Merkle repair of every range at least every 7 days covers the rest. Anything down longer than the 3-hour hint window is rebuilt with a Merkle repair before it serves reads.

Tombstones must outlive the repair cycle. We keep them for gc_grace = 10 days, which is longer than the 7-day repair cycle. If a tombstone were purged before every replica had seen it, a replica that missed the delete would offer the old value during repair, and the deleted data would come back to life.

What would change my mind: a write-mostly table with few deletes and a short TTL on everything can skip scheduled repair, because expiry cleans the data anyway.

deepDives.title: Membership and failure detection
deepDives.problem: Every node must agree, eventually, on who is in the cluster and which tokens they own, and must decide quickly whether a slow peer is dead. Too eager, and a GC pause triggers hints and moves traffic away. Too slow, and requests wait on a dead node.

options.name: Central coordinator (ZooKeeper or etcd)
options.how: Nodes register with ephemeral entries, and everyone watches the membership list.
pros: A single, consistent view
Simple to inspect
cons: Another system whose failure freezes membership changes
A session timeout is a crude failure signal

options.name: Gossip with fixed timeouts
options.how: Each node exchanges heartbeat counters with random peers every second and marks a peer down after 10 s without a heartbeat increase.
pros: No central dependency, spreads in O(log n) rounds
Scales to hundreds of nodes
cons: A fixed timeout is wrong on slow networks and too slow on fast ones

options.name: Gossip with an adaptive (accrual) failure detector
options.how: Each node tracks the arrival-time distribution of a peer's heartbeats and computes a suspicion level that rises the longer one is overdue relative to normal. It marks the peer down above a threshold.
pros: Adapts to each link's normal jitter
One tunable knob that trades detection speed for false alarms
cons: Harder to explain and debug
Still only local opinion: different nodes may disagree for a few seconds

deepDives.choice:
Gossip with an accrual failure detector for liveness, which is purely local and only affects routing and hints. Permanent membership changes (add or remove a node, token moves) are operator actions recorded with a generation number, never inferred from a timeout. A node that is down for an hour is still a member: it gets hints and then a repair, and its data is not re-replicated elsewhere unless an operator replaces it. That avoids moving terabytes because of a flaky switch.

What would change my mind: clusters of several hundred nodes with frequent hardware loss might justify automatic replacement after, say, 30 minutes down, with a cap on how many replacements can run at once.

failures: QUORUM traffic continues on the other 2 replicas. Coordinators keep about 21 GB of hints in total for it and replay them when gossip marks it up. No operator action.
A whole availability zone goes dark

Zone-aware placement means every key loses exactly one replica, so QUORUM reads and writes continue. Clients at ALL fail, which is by design. Hints for that zone's 6 nodes grow fast, so after 3 hours rely on Merkle repair.
A disk dies and a node is replaced with an empty one
The new node takes the same tokens and streams from the surviving replicas, about 0.9 TB. It does not serve reads at ONE until streaming and a repair finish.
Network partition splits zone 1 from zones 2 and 3

Majority side keeps serving QUORUM. The minority side can serve ONE reads, possibly stale, and rejects QUORUM. With sloppy quorum enabled, it would also take writes, which creates siblings or LWW losses to resolve later. That is the CAP trade made explicit.
Caused by purging tombstones before every replica saw them. Keep gc_grace (10 days) longer than the repair cycle (7 days), and alert if any range has gone unrepaired for longer than gc_grace.
All 3 replicas share the load at R = 1 for that table. Better, put a cache in front. The store's own row cache absorbs repeats, but one key can never use more than 3 nodes.
scale: 10× data (42 TB raw, about 180 nodes): same design. Repair cycles take longer, so run repairs on more ranges in parallel. Consider fewer, larger vnodes or fixed partitions to cut per-range overhead.

10× writes (500 000/s): compaction becomes the bottleneck. Pick a compaction strategy per table (size-tiered for write-heavy, leveled for read-heavy), and use more, smaller nodes to spread compaction I/O.

Multiple regions: a full replica set per region, writes at LOCAL_QUORUM, asynchronous cross-region replication, and conflicts resolved by the same per-table mode. Expect seconds of cross-region lag, more during incidents.

followups.q: Why not use Raft or Paxos per partition instead of quorums?
answer: A leader per range gives linearizable reads and writes and safe compare-and-set, which leaderless quorums cannot.
The cost: writes stop for a range until a new leader is elected (about 1–10 s) after a leader failure, and the minority side of a partition cannot write at all.
Pick consensus when correctness of each write matters more than taking writes during failures (metadata, uniqueness). Pick leaderless when availability and latency matter more.

followups.q: A customer needs read-your-writes but wants R = 1 for speed. Options?
answer: Use W = 3 with R = 1 for that table, accepting lower write availability.
Or keep session stickiness: the client sends reads to the coordinator that took its write, and passes the version it wrote so the coordinator can wait or fall back to QUORUM if it has an older one.
Or simply read at QUORUM only for a few seconds after the user's own write.

followups.q: How does a delete work end to end, and why not delete physically?
answer: A delete is a write of a tombstone with a version, replicated like any value.
Physically removing it on some replicas lets a replica that missed the delete resurrect the value during repair.
Compaction drops the tombstone, and the data it shadows, once it is older than gc_grace and every replica has had a repair in between.

followups.q: Values of 20 MB start arriving. What breaks?
answer: Each large write stalls the commit log and memtable flushes, and compaction rewrites those 20 MB many times (10× amplification).
Replica streaming and Merkle leaves become uneven.
Store large blobs in an object store under a content hash and keep only the pointer and metadata in the KV store. Enforce the 1 MB cap at the API.

followups.q: How do you know replicas are actually converging?
answer: Track the age of the last successful repair per range and alert above 7 days.
Measure the read-repair mismatch rate. A rising rate signals dropped hints or a sick node.
Sample keys and compare digests across replicas in the background, reporting the fraction that differ.

mistakes: Claiming R + W > N gives strong consistency, without mentioning failed partial writes, sloppy quorums and concurrent writes.
Choosing last-write-wins without saying that concurrent writes are lost, or relying on wall clocks without discussing skew.
Forgetting tombstones, so deleted data comes back after repair.
Placing replicas without regard to zones, so one zone outage takes 2 of 3 replicas of some keys.
Treating a timeout as a permanent failure and re-replicating terabytes after a 30-second network blip.

mid: Asked about value sizes, consistency needs and behaviour during partitions
Used consistent hashing (not hash mod N) and said why
Replicated each key to 3 nodes and explained what R and W mean
Described what happens on a read when replicas disagree
Mentioned an append-friendly storage engine for the write rate
senior: Stated R + W > N, showed the overlap with a concrete example, and listed what it does not guarantee
Compared LWW and version vectors with a worked example of a concurrent write
Explained hinted handoff, read repair and Merkle-tree repair and when each one applies
Placed replicas across zones and computed quorum availability or node count from the numbers
Handled deletes with tombstones and a grace period tied to the repair cycle
staff: Picked the conflict model per table and explained who writes merge code
Said when they would use consensus per range instead of quorums, and why
Separated liveness detection from membership changes to avoid needless re-replication
Described how to observe convergence in production (repair age, mismatch rate)
